slides.title: Contiguous elements still require a valid shape
keyPoints: Array stride includes each element’s complete size
Rows and columns define indexing meaning
A nearby address is not proof of membership
slides.narration: A matrix stored as two rows of three integers has six elements, but the pair row and column still needs validation before it becomes a linear index. Row one, column two maps to element five using row times three plus column. That arithmetic describes the shape only when the dimensions match the actual storage and both coordinates are in range. An array of structures repeats the whole structure size, including padding, rather than only the useful fields. These rules connect logical indexing to layout. They do not authorize reaching adjacent memory because an address happens to be mapped or because a neighboring value looks plausible.
actions: Translate a valid coordinate into a linear index and then challenge the claimed shape.

question.prompt: Why must dimensions be checked against storage as well as checking row and column?
question.answer: Valid coordinates for a claimed shape can still refer beyond the real storage if that shape is false.

slides.title: Padding is part of layout but not part of the value contract
keyPoints: Members may need alignment gaps
Tail padding supports arrays of the structure
Field equality need not equal raw-byte equality
slides.narration: A structure can contain gaps between members so each member begins at a suitable alignment. It can also have padding at the end so the next element of a structure array is properly aligned. Those bytes contribute to sizeof, but they are not additional named values in the application's record. Comparing whole object representations can therefore disagree with memberwise equality, and sending all bytes can expose data the format never meant to include. Use actual layout tools for supported types and stated ABI assumptions. For a file or network format, encoding each field explicitly usually gives a clearer contract than assuming a native structure matches the external layout.
actions: Draw a record with one alignment gap and explain who, if anyone, owns its meaning.

question.prompt: Why can two structures with equal named members have different raw byte representations?
question.answer: Padding bytes are not necessarily stable semantic data, and object representation can include layout details beyond the named values.

slides.title: Byte order changes interpretation, not the input bytes
keyPoints: The two octets are 02 and 01
Big-endian interpretation weights the first octet by 256
Little-endian interpretation weights the second octet by 256
slides.narration: The array stores the two values two and one in that order. The big-endian expression treats the first as the high octet, computing two times two hundred fifty-six plus one, which is five hundred thirteen. The little-endian expression computes one times two hundred fifty-six plus two, which is two hundred fifty-eight. The final line confirms that the first stored octet remains two. No byte swapping or pointer cast occurs. We explicitly assemble unsigned values, so this demonstration does not depend on the host integer's native byte order. A format must specify which interpretation is correct. Neither convention is inherently the right answer without that agreement.
actions: Predict both decimal results from the two weights before Run.

slides.title: A layout model can explain padding without inventing measurements
keyPoints: The modeled fields have sizes 1, 8, and 2
Each modeled field has an explicit alignment
Changing order changes the modeled total from 24 to 16
slides.narration: This program calculates a declared layout model; it does not inspect an actual compiler's structure. In the first order, the one-byte field ends at offset one, padding advances the eight-byte field to offset eight, and the two-byte field ends at eighteen. Tail padding brings the total to twenty-four. Reordering puts the eight-byte field first, then two bytes, then one, reaching eleven before tail padding brings the total to sixteen. The printed saving is eight bytes per modeled record. This is a derived storage result, not a measured speedup. Reordering a real public structure also changes offsets, so compatibility must be reviewed before applying such a change.
actions: Trace the offsets for each order and clearly label them modeled.

slides.title: Arrays
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Array elements occupy adjacent storage with no extra gap between complete elements beyond each element’s own size.
If the element type includes padding, that padding is included in the stride.
An array of structures therefore repeats the full structure size, not just the sum of useful field bytes.
Contiguity supports efficient traversal and simple address calculations.
slides.narration: Array elements occupy adjacent storage with no extra gap between complete elements beyond each element’s own size. If the element type includes padding, that padding is included in the stride. An array of structures therefore repeats the full structure size, not just the sum of useful field bytes. Contiguity supports efficient traversal and simple address calculations. It also means one out-of-bounds write can reach a neighboring element or another object. The fact that a numeric address lies near valid storage does not make it part of the array. Bounds come from the object, not from what the surrounding memory happens to contain. The element size is sizeof(element_type) . In int a[10] on a platform with four-byte int , the array occupies 40 bytes. In struct Record a[10] , each step uses sizeof(struct Record) , including any tail padding needed to align the next record. A pointer alone does not retain the number of elements. Keep count and capacity with the allocation, or use a container or span. When reading a file of fixed-size records, check both that the total byte count fits and that any required record-size divisibility holds. A leftover partial record is a format error, not an invitation to read beyond the buffer. For a one-dimensional array, address(a[i]) = base + i*sizeof(T) . This is a mathematical address model; source-level pointer arithmetic still requires i to identify an element or the permitted one-past position. To access an element, require i < count . Suppose the base is 0x2000 and each element is eight bytes. Element 5 begins at 0x2028 , because 5 × 8 = 40 = 0x28 . This simple calculation recurs in assembly scaled indexing, structure arrays, file offsets, and cache-line analysis. Always state whether the index counts elements or bytes. A built-in C or C++ array such as int a[3][4] is an array of three arrays, each containing four integers. Its rows are contiguous, and elements within a row are contiguous. With four-byte integers, the address of a[r][c] is modeled as base + (r*4 + c)*4 for valid indices. This is not the same representation as int** , which points to pointers and may describe separately allocated rows. Do not cast between them as a shortcut. For generic matrix interfaces, pass dimensions and strides explicitly or use a suitable multidimensional view. A stride describes layout; it does not itself establish ownership or bounds.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Structures place members in an implementation-defined layout subject to language constraints.
In ordinary C structures, members follow declaration order with possible padding.
C++ standard-layout types provide the predictable subset needed for facilities such as offsetof ; inheritance, virtual functions, and other class features add additional rules.
Use offsetof and sizeof when inspecting a supported type rather than guessing from field names.
slides.narration: Structures place members in an implementation-defined layout subject to language constraints. In ordinary C structures, members follow declaration order with possible padding. C++ standard-layout types provide the predictable subset needed for facilities such as offsetof ; inheritance, virtual functions, and other class features add additional rules. Use offsetof and sizeof when inspecting a supported type rather than guessing from field names. A debugger’s display can show logical members without exposing all padding. When interfacing with hardware or a file format, prefer an explicitly decoded representation over assuming that an ordinary structure matches the external bytes. A type’s alignment constrains the addresses at which its objects may be placed. If a four-byte-aligned member follows a one-byte member, the implementation may insert three padding bytes before it. The enclosing structure’s alignment generally accommodates its most demanding member on the reference ABI. Alignment is both a language validity requirement and an implementation consideration. An x86 instruction’s ability to load an unaligned address does not make an improperly aligned C++ T* access valid. Use byte copying to an aligned object when decoding data at arbitrary byte offsets. Internal padding lies between members; tail padding follows the final member so array elements begin at suitable alignments. Padding bytes do not necessarily have stable values. Comparing whole object representations with memcmp can therefore disagree with memberwise equality. Padding also matters at trust boundaries. Sending an uninitialized structure’s full storage can disclose residual bytes even when every named field has been assigned. Zeroing storage is not a substitute for a stable external format, but explicit field encoding avoids both the layout dependency and accidental padding disclosure.

A tagged union pairs that storage with a discriminator indicating which alternative is active. The discriminator and active object must agree at every interface boundary. Changing the tag without constructing or assigning the appropriate alternative can leave a logically impossible state. In C++, nontrivial member lifetimes make manual unions especially delicate. std::variant packages the tag and lifetime management when its cost and behavior fit the requirement. A union does not create several independent values in the same bytes. It supplies alternative interpretations subject to language rules. Reading a member different from the one most recently established is not a general portable way to reinterpret arbitrary C++ objects. For a representation copy between suitable trivially copyable types of equal size, C++20 provides std::bit_cast ; memcpy is also useful for byte transport. These operations still require valid representations for the intended use. No copying technique can turn arbitrary untrusted bits into a valid pointer or a well-formed complex object merely by avoiding an aliasing violation.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: In little-endian storage, the least significant byte of a multi-byte value is at the lowest address.
A 32-bit value 0x12345678 appears in increasing addresses as 78 56 34 12 .
The reference x86-64 platform uses this ordering for ordinary integer storage.
The numeral 0x12345678 itself has not changed.
slides.narration: In little-endian storage, the least significant byte of a multi-byte value is at the lowest address. A 32-bit value 0x12345678 appears in increasing addresses as 78 56 34 12 . The reference x86-64 platform uses this ordering for ordinary integer storage. The numeral 0x12345678 itself has not changed. Endianness describes the mapping between the value’s bytes and memory addresses, not the written order of digits in a debugger’s integer display. Inspect bytes explicitly when diagnosing a format mismatch. In big-endian storage, the most significant byte is at the lowest address. The same 32-bit value appears as 12 34 56 78 . Many network protocol fields use a specified big-endian order, often called network byte order. A format can also choose little endian or define fields byte by byte. The important property is agreement, not that one order is inherently more correct. Convert at the boundary and keep internal computation in the language’s ordinary value types whenever possible. A portable decoder assembles a value from explicitly ordered bytes. For a four-byte big-endian field, the value is (b0<<24) | (b1<<16) | (b2<<8) | b3 , with each byte converted to a sufficiently wide unsigned type before shifting. The widening is essential. A small byte can undergo signed integer promotion, and shifting into an unsuitable signed range can be invalid in some language modes. A clear decoder validates that four bytes are present, widens them, combines them, and then checks the resulting semantic value. That sequence keeps bounds, representation, and meaning separate.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: “Natural alignment” usually refers to an alignment convenient for a type’s ordinary machine accesses, often related to its width.
It is not one universal language rule saying every n -byte type must be aligned to n bytes.
Query the implementation with _Alignof in C or alignof in C++.
Over-aligned objects require allocation that honors their larger alignment.
slides.narration: “Natural alignment” usually refers to an alignment convenient for a type’s ordinary machine accesses, often related to its width. It is not one universal language rule saying every n -byte type must be aligned to n bytes. Query the implementation with _Alignof in C or alignof in C++. Over-aligned objects require allocation that honors their larger alignment. Ordinary raw byte buffers or a custom allocator may not suffice. A placement construction does not repair an unsuitable address. The storage provider and object constructor must agree on both size and alignment. To round an offset upward to alignment a , a general mathematical expression is ceil(offset/a)*a . For a power-of-two alignment, (offset + a - 1) & ~(a - 1) is a common bitwise form, but the addition must be checked for overflow and a must be nonzero and a power of two. An allocator must account for both the alignment gap and the payload size before returning storage. Rounding first and checking only the payload can miss an overflow or exceed the arena. Chapter 10 develops this as an allocator invariant rather than treating alignment as a cosmetic adjustment. Aligned accesses can reduce the chance of crossing cache-line or page boundaries and may be required by particular instructions. Unaligned accesses on x86-64 are often supported, but their cost depends on width, boundaries, cache state, and instruction choice. “Unaligned is always slow” is too broad, while “x86 allows it, so it is free” is equally misleading. Layout also affects useful bytes per cache line. Reordering members can reduce padding, but changing a public structure can break an ABI or file format. Measure the internal performance benefit and identify every external consumer before changing layout. Correctness and compatibility are constraints on optimization.

keyPoints: Consider a reference-platform structure containing a one-byte kind, a four-byte length aligned to four bytes, and a two-byte flags field aligned to two bytes.

slides.narration: Consider a reference-platform structure containing a one-byte kind, a four-byte length aligned to four bytes, and a two-byte flags field aligned to two bytes. The kind begins at offset 0. Offsets 1 through 3 are padding. The length begins at 4 and occupies four bytes. Flags begins at 8 and occupies two bytes. Two tail-padding bytes make the total size 12 and keep an array’s next element four-byte aligned. Companion listing: ch06/layout.c On the stated reference layout, the output is size=12 align=4 and kind=0 length=4 flags=8 . Reordering the fields as length, flags, kind commonly reduces the size to eight bytes on this ABI: four bytes, then two, then one, then one tail-padding byte. An array of one million records would then use about four million fewer bytes. That is a derived storage saving, not a measured speedup. slides.title: Alignment constrains valid objects, not just speed
keyPoints: Query type alignment rather than guessing
A hardware unaligned load does not settle language validity
Decode arbitrary bytes into a suitable object
slides.narration: An address may be readable by an x86 instruction yet unsuitable for an ordinary C++ object of a particular type. The language's alignment requirement still applies. Natural alignment is not a universal rule that every type aligns to its size; alignof tells us the implementation's requirement. When a protocol field begins at an arbitrary byte offset, casting that byte address to an int pointer is not a general safe decoder. Assemble the value from bytes or copy into an appropriately aligned object under valid representation rules. Performance questions come later: unaligned costs can depend on instruction width and cache or page boundaries, so neither always slow nor always free is a useful universal claim.
actions: Separate the language validity question from the machine performance question.

question.prompt: Why is x86 can load it not enough to justify an int* cast into arbitrary packet bytes?
question.answer: The C++ access still needs a suitably aligned live object and a permitted type interpretation; hardware support answers only part of that contract.

slides.title: A two-dimensional array is not a pointer-to-pointer graph
keyPoints: A built-in matrix contains contiguous row arrays
int** designates pointer objects
Representation changes require a real adapter
slides.narration: A built-in array with three rows of four integers contains three complete row arrays in sequence. Moving a pointer to one row advances by four integers. An int** instead points to pointer objects, often used to reach separately allocated rows. The two layouts are not interchangeable because one contains integers directly where the other expects addresses. A cast changes an access type but does not construct the missing pointer objects or establish valid rows. A flexible matrix interface can carry dimensions and strides explicitly. That makes the layout contract visible and allows a caller to represent contiguous or other supported arrangements without pretending incompatible storage has the same shape.
actions: Draw three row arrays and then a separate array of three row pointers.

question.prompt: Why is casting a contiguous matrix to int** not a correct conversion?
question.answer: The contiguous matrix does not contain the row-pointer objects that int** access expects. The cast cannot create them.

slides.title: Overlapping storage needs a valid active alternative
keyPoints: Union members share space
A tag must match the active object
Representation copying is not arbitrary object construction
slides.narration: A union saves space by allowing alternatives to overlap, but it does not give independent simultaneous values to all members. The program must know which member is active and respect its lifetime. A tagged union keeps a discriminator beside that storage; a mismatch between the tag and active object is an invalid state. std::variant manages that relationship for many C++ uses. For inspecting a representation, bit_cast or byte copying has a different purpose and specific restrictions. Neither technique turns arbitrary incoming bits into a valid pointer or a well-formed complex object. Choose the operation that matches the goal: alternative values, representation inspection, or validated external decoding.
actions: Ask learners to distinguish a tagged alternative from a byte decoder.

question.prompt: Does copying arbitrary bytes into storage establish a meaningful pointer object for later dereference?
question.answer: No. Representation transport does not prove that the bits designate a valid live object or satisfy the intended access contract.

slides.title: Validate bytes, decode values, then validate meaning
keyPoints: Check the required extent first
Widen octets before shifting
Check the decoded domain after assembling the value
slides.narration: A four-octet field can be assembled by shifting each octet into its declared position and combining the pieces. Before that, four octets must actually be available. The octets should be converted to a sufficiently wide unsigned type before the shifts so promotions do not create an unintended narrow or signed operation. After assembly, the result may still violate the protocol's semantic rule, such as a length larger than the message allows. These are three separate checks: available representation, valid arithmetic construction, and accepted meaning. Keeping them in that order makes a parser easier to debug because each rejection names a different failed promise.
actions: Trace a four-byte length that is syntactically complete but exceeds a stated payload limit.

question.prompt: Can successfully assembling four bytes prove that the decoded length is acceptable?
question.answer: No. It proves a value was formed from the available bytes. The protocol’s semantic size limit still needs checking.

slides.title: Smaller storage can be useful and still break compatibility
keyPoints: Reordering may reduce padding
Public offsets can be part of an ABI
Derived byte savings are not measured speedup
slides.narration: The layout model saved eight bytes per record. Across one million modeled records, that is eight million bytes under the same assumptions. It still does not tell us elapsed time or cache behavior on a real workload. More seriously, changing member order changes offsets that separately compiled code or a raw-file format may rely on. Internal types can sometimes be changed with coordinated rebuilding; public binary interfaces need an explicit compatibility plan. Review the consumers before optimizing layout. Then measure the property that motivated the change instead of claiming that fewer bytes automatically implies a fixed speed increase.
actions: Distinguish the eight-million-byte arithmetic estimate from a real timing claim.

question.prompt: What must be checked before reordering members in a published structure?
question.answer: Every ABI or external-format consumer that depends on member offsets, size, or alignment, plus the actual performance or storage goal.

slides.title: Carry units and ownership with the layout calculation
keyPoints: Indices count elements
Offsets and sizes may count bytes
A view describes storage but does not own it
slides.narration: A layout formula becomes easier to review when every number has a unit. Row times column count produces an element index. Multiplying by an element size produces a byte offset. A pointer operation scales in elements of its pointed-to type. Confusing these units can multiply a size twice or omit scaling entirely. A view that stores dimensions and strides still borrows a live owner; correct arithmetic does not extend its lifetime. In a real system, keep these contracts together in the interface and test both valid edges and rejected shapes. The goal is a representation that another maintainer can explain without guessing at hidden layout assumptions.
actions: Ask learners to annotate one matrix formula with units at each step.

question.prompt: Does a correct byte-offset formula alone prove a view remains usable?
question.answer: No. The underlying owner must still be alive, the shape must match storage, and the requested access must satisfy type and alignment rules.
